claim: MreB from Geobacillus stearothermophilus (MreBGs) forms straight pairs of protofilaments on lipid surfaces in the presence of ATP or GTP.
source: We show that Geobacillus stearothermophilus MreB forms straight pairs of protofilaments on lipid surfaces in the presence of ATP or GTP, but not in the presence of ADP, GDP or non-hydrolysable ATP analogs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations showing filament formation under specified conditions (Figure 2A, Figure 3A).

claim: MreBGs does not form straight pairs of protofilaments on lipid surfaces in the presence of ADP, GDP or non-hydrolysable ATP analogs.
source: We show that Geobacillus stearothermophilus MreB forms straight pairs of protofilaments on lipid surfaces in the presence of ATP or GTP, but not in the presence of ADP, GDP or non-hydrolysable ATP analogs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy showing absence of filaments under these conditions (Figure 3A).

claim: Membrane anchoring of MreBGs is mediated by two spatially close short hydrophobic sequences.
source: We demonstrate that membrane anchoring is mediated by two spatially close short hydrophobic sequences while electrostatic interactions also contribute to lipid binding
evidence: Supported by experimental data from deletion mutants and QCM-D experiments (Figure 4).

claim: Electrostatic interactions contribute to lipid binding of MreBGs.
source: We demonstrate that membrane anchoring is mediated by two spatially close short hydrophobic sequences while electrostatic interactions also contribute to lipid binding
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D experiments with different lipid compositions (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).

claim: The population of membrane-bound protofilament doublets of MreBGs is in steady-state.
source: and show that the population of membrane-bound protofilament doublets is in steady-state.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from kinetic experiments with limiting ATP concentrations (Figure 5B).

claim: In solution, MreBGs protofilament doublets were not detected in any condition tested.
source: In solution, protofilament doublets were not detected in any condition tested.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: In solution, MreBGs formed large sheets regardless of the bound nucleotide, albeit at a higher critical concentration.
source: Instead, MreB formed large sheets regardless of the bound nucleotide, albeit at a higher critical concentration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations at high MreB concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Both lipids and ATP are facilitators of MreB polymerization.
source: Altogether, our results indicate that both lipids and ATP are facilitators of MreB polymerization
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations showing enhanced polymerization in the presence of both lipids and ATP (Figure 2A, Figure 3A).

claim: ATP hydrolysis promotes both membrane binding and filaments assembly/disassembly of MreBGs.
source: and are consistent with a dual effect of ATP hydrolysis, in promoting both membrane binding and filaments assembly/disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from QCM-D experiments showing ATP-dependent membrane binding and kinetic experiments showing steady-state dynamics (Figure 3C, Figure 5B).

claim: The crystal structure of apo MreBGs was solved at 1.8 Å resolution.
source: The purified MreBGs protein was crystallized and the structure of its apo form was solved at 1.8 Å resolution (Protein Data Bank Identifier (PDB ID) 7ZPT).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from X-ray crystallography (Supplementary file 1).

claim: Monomers of apo MreBGs display the canonical fold of actin-like proteins, characterized by four subdomains IA, IIA, IB and IIB.
source: Monomers of apo MreBGs display the canonical fold of actin-like proteins, characterized by four subdomains IA, IIA, IB and IIB (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis (Figure 1A).

claim: One of the most similar structures to apo MreBGs is the apo form of MreBTm (PDB ID 1JCF; van den Ent et al., 2001), with a root mean square deviation (rmsd) of 1.92 Å over 305 superimposed Cα atoms and a Z-score of 16.0.
source: One of the most similar structures to apo MreBGs is the apo form of MreBTm (PDB ID 1JCF; van den Ent et al., 2001), with a root mean square deviation (rmsd) of 1.92 Å over 305 superimposed Cα atoms and a Z-score of 16.0.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from structural comparison analysis.

claim: MreBGs is in a slightly more open conformation than MreBTm, mainly due to a movement of domain IB.
source: Superimposition of the two proteins (Figure 1A) revealed that MreBGs is in a slightly more open conformation than MreBTm, mainly due to a movement of domain IB, which is the less conserved within the actin superfamily of proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from structural comparison (Figure 1A).

claim: Loop β6-α2, which connects subdomains IA and IB and closes the nucleotide-binding pocket, is partially disordered in apo MreBGs.
source: Loop β6-α2, which connects subdomains IA and IB and closes the nucleotide-binding pocket, is partially disordered in apo MreBGs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis.

claim: The hydrophobic loop α2-β7 in MreBGs displays a distinct conformation, packed on the N-terminal extremity of the polypeptide chain.
source: In domain IA, the hydrophobic loop α2-β7, which has been shown to be involved in MreBTm membrane binding (Salje et al., 2011) and is 2 residues longer in MreBGs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), displays a distinct conformation, packed on the N-terminal extremity of the polypeptide chain.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis and comparison with MreBTm structure (Salje et al., 2011).

claim: Crystal packing analysis of MreBGs revealed straight protofilaments characterized by a subunit repeat distance of 51 Å.
source: Crystal packing analysis revealed straight protofilaments characterized by a subunit repeat distance of 51 Å (Figure 1B), similar to that observed in crystal structures of other actin homologs (Harne et al., 2020; Pande et al., 2022; Roeben et al., 2006; van den Ent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis (Figure 1B) and comparison with other actin homologs (Harne et al., 2020; Pande et al., 2022; Roeben et al., 2006; van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: In the ATP-bound state of MreBGs, domain IB interacts with domain IA.
source: However, because of the open conformation of MreBGs (Figure 1A), domain IB interacts with domain IA (Figure 1C) and not with domain IIA as observed for example for MreBTm (Figure 1D; van den Ent et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis (Figure 1C) and comparison with MreBTm (van den Ent et al., 2001).

claim: In vivo, MreBBs forms membrane-associated nanofilaments.
source: In vivo, MreBBs forms membrane-associated nanofilaments (Billaudeau et al., 2019; Hussain et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Billaudeau et al., 2019; Hussain et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2001).

claim: MreB filaments from Gram-negative bacteria have an intrinsic affinity for membranes.
source: and MreB filaments from Gram-negative bacteria have been shown to have an intrinsic affinity for membranes (Garenne et al., 2020; Maeda et al., 2012; Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Garenne et al., 2020; Maeda et al., 2012; Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: In the presence of both ATP and lipids, MreBGs formed a lawn of double protofilaments in 100% of fields.
source: Using a semi-quantitative workflow analysis of TEM grids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Materials and methods), we found that in the presence of both ATP and lipids, MreBGs formed a lawn of double protofilaments in 100% of fields
evidence: Supported by experimental data from quantitative TEM analysis (Figure 2A).

claim: Only 4% and 8% of the fields contained polymers in the absence of either ATP or lipids, respectively.
source: while only 4% and 8% of the fields contained polymers (often at very low density) in the absence of either ATP or lipids, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from quantitative TEM analysis (Figure 2A).

claim: Polymers were observed on a lipid monolayer at a concentration of MreB above 0.55 µM (0.02 mg/mL), for a theoretical critical concentration of ~0.45 µM.
source: On a lipid monolayer, polymers were observed at a concentration of MreB above 0.55 µM (0.02 mg/mL), for a theoretical critical concentration of ~0.45 µM (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from concentration-dependent polymerization assays (Figure 2B).

claim: The critical concentration of MreBGs is very similar to the critical concentration reported for ATP-MreBTm.
source: which is very similar to the critical concentration reported for ATP-MreBTm (Bean and Amann, 2008).
evidence: Supported by comparison with published data (Bean and Amann, 2008).

claim: Pairs of MreBGs protofilaments are generally straight, and single protofilaments were never observed.
source: Pairs of MreBGs protofilaments are generally straight, and single protofilaments were never observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations.

claim: The diffraction patterns of MreBGs sheets showed a longitudinal repeat of 54 Å and a lateral spacing of ~37 Å.
source: The diffraction patterns of the sheets showed a longitudinal repeat of 54 Å and a lateral spacing of ~37 Å (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Fourier transform analysis of EM images (Figure 2D).

claim: 2D averaging of negatively stained EM images of 1 554 individual pairs of filaments confirmed a longitudinal subunit repeat of 54 Å and refined the lateral subunit repeat to 31 Å.
source: 2D averaging of negatively stained EM images of 1 554 individual pairs of filaments (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4) confirmed a longitudinal subunit repeat of 54 Å and refined the lateral subunit repeat to 31 Å
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 2D image processing (Figure 2E).

claim: At 100 mM KCl, LUVs decorated with MreBGs filaments displayed inward bending (negatively curved areas) where MreBGs filaments accumulated.
source: At 100 mM KCl (our standard polymerization condition), LUVs displayed inward bending (negatively curved areas) where MreBGs filaments accumulated (arrows in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cryo-EM observations (Figure 2F).

claim: At 500 mM KCl, MreBGs readily polymerized into straight pairs of filaments which faceted and tubulated the liposomes.
source: At 500 mM KCl, MreBGs readily polymerized into straight pairs of filaments as well, which also distorted liposomes but did not induce negative curvature. Instead, they faceted and tubulated the liposomes (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 5C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cryo-EM observations (Figure 2G).

claim: High salt concentration increases the stiffness of MreB filaments and/or of the membrane.
source: suggesting that high salt concentration increases the stiffness of MreB filaments and/or of the membrane.
evidence: Inferred from observations of different liposome deformation patterns at different salt concentrations (Figure 2F-G).

claim: Specific binding of cations at discrete sites along the filament has been shown to stiffen actin filaments, determining their bending rigidity.
source: Specific binding of cations at discrete sites along the filament has been shown to stiffen actin filaments, determining their bending rigidity (Kang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Kang et al., 2012).

claim: MreBGs formed straight pairs of protofilaments and sheets in the presence of either ATP or GTP.
source: MreBGs formed straight pairs of protofilaments and sheets in the presence of either ATP or GTP, as shown by negative stain EM (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations (Figure 3A).

claim: The average length of MreBGs double filaments displayed an approximately twofold increase in the presence of GTP compared to ATP.
source: Noteworthy, the average length of double filaments displayed an approximately twofold increase in the presence of GTP compared to ATP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from filament length measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Virtually no double filaments were observed when ATP/GTP was replaced by ADP, GDP, AMP-PNP, or ApCpp, either in the presence or in the absence of lipids, in standard polymerization conditions.
source: Virtually no double filaments were observed when ATP/GTP was replaced by ADP, GDP, AMP-PNP, or ApCpp (5′‐adenylyl methylenediphosphate), either in the presence or in the absence of lipids, in our standard polymerization conditions (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations (Figure 3A).

claim: Increasing amounts of AMP-PNP efficiently decreased the presence of MreBGs filaments on the EM grids in a competition experiment with ATP.
source: Next, we performed a competition experiment by mixing ATP (1 mM) with increasing amounts of AMP-PNP (1, 10 and 25 mM) in the polymerization reaction. Increasing amounts of AMP-PNP efficiently decreased the presence of MreBGs filaments on the EM grids (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from competition experiments (Figure 3B).

claim: AMP-PNP binds to MreBGs but does not support efficient polymerization on a lipid surface.
source: We concluded that AMP-PNP binds to MreBGs but does not support efficient polymerization on a lipid surface.
evidence: Inferred from competition experiments showing AMP-PNP can compete with ATP but does not promote polymerization (Figure 3B).

claim: At the highest MreBGs concentration tested (6.98 µM), efficient formation of double filaments on the lipid monolayer was still observed only in the presence of ATP.
source: At the highest MreBGs concentration that we could test in our experimental conditions (6.98 µM), about 15-fold the estimated ATP-MreBGs critical concentration (0.45 µM, Figure 2B), efficient formation of double filaments on the lipid monolayer was still observed only in the presence of ATP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from concentration-dependent polymerization assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: ADP-MreBGs double filaments were more frequent at higher MreB concentration, indicating a higher critical concentration required for filament formation.
source: Although still scarce, ADP-MreBGs double filaments were nevertheless more frequent at higher MreB concentration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), indicating a higher critical concentration required for filament formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from concentration-dependent polymerization assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: At high MreB concentrations, large sheet- and ribbon-like structures became frequent in the presence of ADP and very frequent in the presence of AMP-PNP.
source: Surprisingly, at high MreB concentrations, the large sheet- and ribbon-like structures observed to form in the bulk solution at very low frequency in the presence of ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C) became frequent in the presence of ADP and very frequent in the presence of AMP-PNP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: The Fourier transforms of the sheet-like structures formed in solution showed sets of discrete reflections, with diffraction equatorial spots of about 6.5 nm.
source: The Fourier transforms of the sheet-like structures formed in these conditions showed sets of discrete reflections, with diffraction equatorial spots of about 6.5 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Fourier transform analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Membrane binding induces conformational changes in MreB filaments.
source: larger than the repeats found on membrane-bound sheets, suggesting that membrane binding induces conformational changes in MreB filaments, as previously suggested (Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of diffraction patterns in solution versus on membranes, and supported by citation (Shi et al., 2020).

claim: Nucleotide hydrolysis is not strictly required for filament formation of MreBGs.
source: The presence of ADP- and AMP-PNP-MreBGs sheets in solution indicated that nucleotide hydrolysis is not strictly required for filament formation.
evidence: Inferred from observation of sheet formation in the presence of non-hydrolyzable nucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: ATP hydrolysis promotes efficient filament formation of MreBGs at the membrane.
source: However, the formation of extended sheets in solution concomitant with the absence of double protofilaments on a lipid surface in the presence of ADP or AMP-PNP, suggests that ATP hydrolysis promotes efficient filament formation at the membrane.
evidence: Inferred from differential polymerization behavior in solution versus on membranes with different nucleotides (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Binding of MreBGs to SLBs was strongly dependent on ATP.
source: Binding was strongly dependent on ATP and was substantially affected by the lipid composition of SLBs (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: Increasing the levels of DOPG in SLBs led to a higher amount of MreBGs binding.
source: Increasing the levels of DOPG led to a higher amount of MreBGs binding, with DOPC:PG 80:20 giving the highest observed adsorption, suggesting that the presence of negatively charged lipids favors MreBGs binding to the membrane.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements with different lipid compositions (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).

claim: In the presence of ATP, binding of MreBGs to SLBs was detected almost instantaneously after adding MreBGs for all concentrations tested.
source: In the presence of ATP, binding was detected almost instantaneously after adding MreBGs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, closed arrows) for all concentrations of MreB tested, either above or below the concentration in which polymers were observed by EM on a lipid monolayer (0.55 µM) (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: A shift in frequency was detected even at 0.1 µM MreB, well below the critical ATP-MreB concentration, suggesting that MreB monomers might bind to SLBs.
source: Interestingly, a shift in frequency was detected even at 0.1 µM MreB, well below the critical ATP-MreB concentration, suggesting that MreB monomers might bind too (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and E, F).
evidence: Inferred from QCM-D measurements showing binding below the critical concentration (Figure 3C).

claim: When replacing ATP with ADP or AMP-PNP, no significant binding of MreBGs to SLBs was detected at either low or high concentrations of MreB.
source: When replacing ATP with ADP or AMP-PNP, we were not able to detect any significant binding at either low or high concentrations of MreB, indicating a virtually complete loss of interaction (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: Higher concentrations of ADP and AMP-PNP did not restore the binding of MreBGs to the SLBs.
source: We further increased the concentration of ADP or AMP-PNP to exclude the possibility that the binding was simply affected by a decreased affinity of MreBGs for these nucleotides. Higher concentrations of ADP and AMP-PNP did not restore the binding of MreBGs to the SLBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements with high nucleotide concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).

claim: Nucleotide hydrolysis drives MreBGs membrane binding.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that nucleotide hydrolysis drives MreBGs membrane binding.
evidence: Inferred from QCM-D experiments showing ATP-dependent but not ADP/AMP-PNP-dependent binding (Figure 3C).

claim: The thickness of the MreB films on SLBs ranged from 0.1 nm to approximately 4 nm, which corresponds to ~2.5% to 100% coverage assuming a monolayer filament thickness.
source: The thickness of the MreB films ranged from 0.1 nm to approximately 4 nm on the SLBs with an 80:20 ratio of DOPC:DOPG, which corresponds to ~2.5% to 100% coverage assuming a monolayer filament thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H and Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements and Sauerbrey model calculations (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H).

claim: Membrane binding of MreBTm is mediated by a small loop containing two hydrophobic residues (L93 and F94).
source: Membrane binding of MreBTm is mediated by a small loop containing two hydrophobic residues (L93 and F94), whereas binding of MreBEc and MreBCc is mediated by an amino-terminal extension (9 residues) predicted as an amphipathic helix, which is disordered in all crystal structures of MreBCc (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, green highlights).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: Binding of MreBEc and MreBCc is mediated by an amino-terminal extension (9 residues) predicted as an amphipathic helix.
source: Membrane binding of MreBTm is mediated by a small loop containing two hydrophobic residues (L93 and F94), whereas binding of MreBEc and MreBCc is mediated by an amino-terminal extension (9 residues) predicted as an amphipathic helix, which is disordered in all crystal structures of MreBCc (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, green highlights).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: The N-terminal extension of MreBEc is essential to MreB function in E. coli.
source: Albeit essential to MreB function in E. coli (Salje et al., 2011), this N-terminal extension is not required for polymerization in vitro (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Salje et al., 2011).

claim: The N-terminal extension of MreBEc is not required for polymerization in vitro.
source: Albeit essential to MreB function in E. coli (Salje et al., 2011), this N-terminal extension is not required for polymerization in vitro (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: MreBBs was not predicted to carry an N-terminal amphipathic helix.
source: MreBBs was not predicted to carry an N-terminal amphipathic helix (Salje et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Salje et al., 2011).

claim: N-terminal amphipathic helices are a conserved feature of the Proteobacteria phylum and most Gram-negative bacteria, but are absent in Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes species.
source: A systematic search in a large panel of MreB proteins spanning over the entire bacterial kingdom revealed that N-terminal amphipathic helices are a conserved feature of the Proteobacteria phylum and most Gram-negative bacteria, but are absent in Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes species (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sequence analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Most Firmicutes, including Bacilli (MreBGs and MreBBs) and Clostridia, possess a shorter N-terminal sequence containing 4–7 hydrophobic amino-acids.
source: Most Firmicutes, including Bacilli (MreBGs and MreBBs) and Clostridia, but with the notable exception of the wall-less Mollicutes, possess a shorter N-terminal sequence containing 4–7 hydrophobic amino-acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sequence analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: In the crystal structure of the apo form of MreBGs, the short hydrophobic N-terminal sequence is in close proximity to loop α2-β7.
source: We noticed that in the crystal structure of the apo form of MreBGs this short hydrophobic N-terminal sequence is in close proximity to loop α2-β7 (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis (Figure 1A).

claim: A cluster of positively charged residues surrounds the protruding hydrophobic subdomain formed by the α2-β7 loop and the N-terminal sequence in MreBGs.
source: Interestingly, analysis of the crystal structure of MreBGs also showed that a cluster of positively charged residues surrounds the protruding hydrophobic subdomain formed by the α2-β7 loop and the N-terminal sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Membrane binding of MreBGs may result from both ionic and hydrophobic interactions.
source: Since our QCM-D data suggested that anionic lipids favor MreBGs binding to a lipid bilayer, we hypothesized that membrane binding may result from both ionic and hydrophobic interactions, with the positively charged residues that cluster around the membrane insertion hydrophobic region interacting with negatively charged lipids.
evidence: Inferred from QCM-D data showing lipid composition effects and structural analysis showing charged residues (Figure 3C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Folding of MreBGs was not affected by deletions of the α2-β7 loop and/or N-terminal sequence as shown by circular dichroism.
source: Folding of the protein was not affected by the deletions as shown by circular dichroism (CD) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from circular dichroism measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: The three mutants (ΔGLFA, ΔNter, and ΔNter+ΔGLFA) displayed a dramatic reduction in the formation of double filaments on lipid surfaces relative to the wild-type at high salt concentration (500 mM KCl).
source: The three mutants displayed a dramatic reduction in the formation of double filaments in the EM fields relative to the wild-type, with a gradation of defects, with the deletion of the GLFA sequence having the least effect and the double deletion having the greatest (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations (Figure 4A).

claim: A similar gradient of phenotypes was observed for the mutants at lower salt concentration (100 mM KCl) but the overall number of filaments detected on the membrane surface was increased.
source: A similar gradient of phenotypes was observed at lower salt concentration (100 mM KCl) but the overall number of filaments detected on the membrane surface was increased as expected, consistent with electrostatic interactions also contributing to lipid binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).

claim: Under the same polymerization conditions, no filaments were detected in solution for any of the mutants.
source: Under the same polymerization conditions, no filaments were detected in solution for any of the mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A), arguing against the possibility that the mutants could form filaments in solution but that they are impaired for membrane binding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).

claim: Membrane adsorption of the three mutants in the presence of ATP was strongly reduced relative to the wild-type protein in QCM-D experiments.
source: In QCM-D experiments, membrane adsorption in the presence of ATP was strongly reduced in the three mutants relative to the wild-type protein, mirroring the polymerization assays at either high- or low-salt concentration (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements (Figure 4B).

claim: High salt reduced membrane binding of MreBGs relative to low salt in all conditions.
source: High salt reduced membrane binding relative to low salt in all conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).

claim: In the presence of ADP, binding was not observed for any of the mutants.
source: In the presence of ADP, binding was not observed for any of the mutants, as previously observed with the wild-type protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from QCM-D measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).

claim: The spatially close hydrophobic N-terminus and α2-β7 loop are membrane anchors of MreBGs filaments.
source: Taken together, these results show that the spatially close hydrophobic N-terminus and α2-β7 loop are membrane anchors of MreBGs filaments
evidence: Inferred from deletion mutant experiments showing reduced membrane binding and polymerization (Figure 4).

claim: Electrostatic interactions are involved in lipid binding of MreBGs.
source: and further confirm that electrostatic interactions are also involved in lipid binding.
evidence: Inferred from salt concentration effects on membrane binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).

claim: The crystal structure of ATP-bound MreBGs was solved at 2.3 Å resolution.
source: In order to test the impact of nucleotide binding, we co-crystallized MreBGs with ATP and solved the crystal structure of the complex at 2.3 Å resolution (PDB ID 8AZG).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from X-ray crystallography (Supplementary file 1).

claim: The electron density map of ATP-bound MreBGs clearly revealed the presence of three phosphates, demonstrating that the ATP had not been hydrolyzed into ADP.
source: The electron density map clearly revealed the presence of three phosphates, demonstrating that the ATP had not been hydrolyzed into ADP (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).

claim: The absence of a Mg2+ ion in the catalytic site of ATP-bound MreBGs is probably why ATP was not hydrolyzed.
source: This is probably due to the absence of a Mg2+ ion in the catalytic site. No residual electron density peak could be interpreted as a Mg2+ ion with appropriate coordination.
evidence: Inferred from crystal structure analysis showing no Mg2+ ion.

claim: The structure of the ATP-bound form of MreBGs is highly similar to the apo form, with a rmsd of 1.41 Å over 313 aligned Cα atoms.
source: The structure of the ATP-bound form of MreBGs is highly similar to the apo form, with a rmsd of 1.41 Å over 313 aligned Cα atoms (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from structural comparison (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).

claim: ATP binding induced a small closure of the nucleotide-binding pocket in MreBGs.
source: However, ATP binding induced a small closure of the nucleotide-binding pocket, and loop β6-α2, which was disordered in the apo structure, is fully visible in the electron density map.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure comparison.

claim: Loop β6-α2, which was disordered in the apo structure of MreBGs, is fully visible in the electron density map of the ATP-bound structure.
source: However, ATP binding induced a small closure of the nucleotide-binding pocket, and loop β6-α2, which was disordered in the apo structure, is fully visible in the electron density map.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure comparison.

claim: The hydrophobic loop α2-β7 and the N-terminus display an alternative conformation in the ATP-bound structure of MreBGs compared to the apo structure.
source: The hydrophobic loop α2-β7 and the N-terminus also display an alternative conformation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure comparison (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).

claim: MreBs of several Gram-negative bacteria have been shown to slowly hydrolyze ATP in solution.
source: MreBs of several Gram-negative bacteria have been shown to slowly hydrolyze ATP in solution (Bean and Amann, 2008; Esue et al., 2005; Esue et al., 2006; Gaballah et al., 2011; Mayer and Amann, 2009; Nurse and Marians, 2013; Pande et al., 2022; Popp et al., 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Bean and Amann, 2008; Esue et al., 2005; Esue et al., 2006; Gaballah et al., 2011; Mayer and Amann, 2009; Nurse and Marians, 2013; Pande et al., 2022; Popp et al., 2010b).

claim: In standard polymerization conditions, in the absence of lipids and at 53 °C, MreBGs showed a constant release of Pi over time, with an equilibrium rate of Pi dissociation of 0.198±0.008 Pi/min/MreB molecule.
source: In our standard polymerization conditions, in the absence of lipids and at 53 °C (a temperature close to the optimal growth temperature of G. stearothermophilus), we observed a constant release of Pi over time, with an equilibrium rate of Pi dissociation of 0.198±0.008 Pi/min/MreB molecule (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays (Figure 5A).

claim: The rate of Pi release by MreBGs was reduced approximately threefold in the absence of lipids, to 0.068±0.02 Pi/min/MreB molecule.
source: The rate was reduced approximately threefold, to 0.068±0.02 Pi/min/MreB molecule in the absence of lipids (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays (Figure 5A).

claim: At 500 mM KCl, similar rates of Pi release were observed for MreBGs, with 0.158±0.003 and 0.081±0.004 Pi/min/MreB with and without lipids, respectively.
source: Similar rates were observed when the incubations were performed at a higher KCl concentration (500 mM), with 0.158±0.003 and 0.081±0.004 Pi/min/MreB with and without lipids, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-E).

claim: Pi release rates of MreBGs were decreased when incubations were performed at 37 °C instead of 53 °C, but the rate of Pi release remained comparatively higher in the presence of lipids.
source: As expected, Pi release rates were decreased when incubations were performed at 37 °C instead of 53 °C, but the rate of Pi release remained comparatively higher in the presence of lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays at different temperatures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The rates of Pi release by MreBGs in the presence of ATP (~1 Pi/MreB in 5 min at 53 °C) are comparable to those observed for MreBTm and MreBEc in vitro.
source: These rates of Pi release in the presence of ATP (~1 Pi/MreB in 5 min at 53 °C) are comparable to those observed for MreBTm and MreBEc in vitro (Esue et al., 2005; Esue et al., 2006; Nurse and Marians, 2013)
evidence: Supported by comparison with published data (Esue et al., 2005; Esue et al., 2006; Nurse and Marians, 2013).

claim: The rate of Pi release by MreBGs is remarkably similar to the rate of the (very slow) dissociation of γ-phosphate after ATP hydrolysis within actin filaments, which has a half-time of ∼6 min.
source: and also remarkably similar to the rate of the (very slow) dissociation of γ-phosphate after ATP hydrolysis within actin filaments, which has a half-time of ∼6 min (Carlier and Pantaloni, 1986).
evidence: Supported by comparison with published data on actin (Carlier and Pantaloni, 1986).

claim: The release of Pi by MreBGs was constant over the length of the ATPase experiments.
source: Interestingly, the release of Pi was constant over the length of our ATPase experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from kinetic ATPase assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Similar density and lengths of negatively stained MreBGs polymers were observed over the EM grids for all incubation (polymerization) times tested, ranging from a few minutes to several hours.
source: However, similar density and lengths of negatively stained MreBGs polymers were observed over the EM grids for all incubation (polymerization) times tested, ranging from a few minutes to several hours.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from electron microscopy observations at different time points.

claim: A similar density of double protofilaments was observed on the lipid monolayer at early time points at both saturating and limiting concentrations of ATP.
source: As shown in Figure 5B a similar density of double protofilaments was observed on the lipid monolayer at early time points at both saturating and limiting concentrations of ATP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from kinetic polymerization experiments (Figure 5B).

claim: Polymers progressively disappeared over time in the presence of limiting concentrations of ATP, but not when ATP was in excess.
source: However, polymers progressively disappeared over time in the presence of limiting concentrations of ATP, but not when ATP was in excess.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from kinetic polymerization experiments (Figure 5B).

claim: MreB polymerization on a lipid surface is a dynamic process, with steady-state polymerization/depolymerization rates.
source: These observations suggest that MreB polymerization on a lipid surface is a dynamic process, with steady-state polymerization/depolymerization rates.
evidence: Inferred from kinetic experiments showing polymer disappearance with limiting ATP (Figure 5B).

claim: MreBGs releases Pi after hydrolysis of GTP as efficiently as after hydrolysis of ATP, both in the presence and in the absence of lipids.
source: We found that MreBGs also releases Pi after hydrolysis of GTP as efficiently as after hydrolysis of ATP, both in the presence and in the absence of lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase/GTPase activity assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The specific ATPase activity of the three mutants and of the wild-type MreBGs reflected their polymerization and QCM-D assays at either high- or low-salt concentration.
source: Finally, the specific ATPase activity of the three mutants impaired for membrane binding and of the wild-type MreBGs reflected their polymerization and QCM-D assays at either high- or low-salt concentration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays of mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).

claim: In the absence of lipids, all MreBGs proteins (wild-type and mutants) released Pi at comparative rates, suggesting that a basal level of ATP degradation occurs in solution.
source: In the absence of lipids, all proteins released Pi at comparative rates, suggesting that a basal level of ATP degradation occurs in solution.
evidence: Inferred from ATPase activity assays showing similar rates without lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).

claim: In the presence of lipids, the rate of Pi release of all mutants was reduced relative to the wild-type MreBGs.
source: In the presence of lipids, the rate of Pi release of all mutants was reduced relative to the wild-type MreBGs
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).

claim: Overall Pi release rates were significantly reduced at high salt (500 mM KCl) relative to low salt (100 mM KCl).
source: and overall Pi release rates were significantly reduced at high salt (500 mM KCl) relative to low salt (100 mM KCl) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays at different salt concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).

claim: At 100 mM KCl, the mutant deleted for both the GLFA and the N-terminus hydrophobic sequences was the only one severely impacted in Pi release rate.
source: At 100 mM KCl, the mutant deleted for both the GLFA and the N-terminus hydrophobic sequences was the only one severely impacted in Pi release rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ATPase activity assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The release of Pi by the wild-type and membrane-binding mutants in the presence of lipids was consistent with the density of double filaments observed in the EM fields.
source: We concluded that the release of Pi by the wild-type and membrane-binding mutants in the presence of lipids was consistent with the density of double filaments observed in the EM fields.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between ATPase activity and polymerization observations.

claim: The presence of lipids is not required for the ATPase/GTPase activity of MreBGs.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the presence of lipids is not required for the ATPase/GTPase activity of MreBGs.
evidence: Inferred from observation of Pi release in the absence of lipids (Figure 5A).

claim: Pi release by MreBGs is enhanced in the presence of lipids.
source: However, Pi release is enhanced in the presence of lipids, advocating for some conformational changes upon binding of MreBGs to the membrane and/or upon polymerization on the lipid surface.
evidence: Inferred from higher Pi release rates in the presence of lipids (Figure 5A).

claim: Pairs of filaments formed on a lipid surface are at steady-state, undergoing a dynamic, ATP-driven assembly/disassembly process.
source: Furthermore, we show that pairs of filaments formed on a lipid surface are at steady-state, undergoing a dynamic, ATP-driven assembly/disassembly process.
evidence: Inferred from kinetic experiments showing polymer disappearance with limiting ATP (Figure 5B).

claim: If individual double filaments of MreBGs are antiparallel, they are structurally nonpolar and thus their disassembly could result either from dynamic instability or from steady-state fluctuations (growing and shrinking) of the filaments ends.
source: If individual double filaments are antiparallel (van den Ent et al., 2014), they are structurally nonpolar and thus their disassembly could result either from dynamic instability or from steady-state fluctuations (growing and shrinking) of the filaments ends.
evidence: Inferred from structural considerations and citation to previous work (van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: The requirement for a membrane is consistent with the observation that in vivo MreB polymeric assemblies are membrane-associated (i.e. localize at the cell periphery).
source: The requirement for a membrane is consistent with the observation that in vivo MreB polymeric assemblies are membrane-associated (i.e. localize at the cell periphery), in line with their role as scaffold of the CW elongation machinery.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro observations and established knowledge of in vivo MreB localization.

claim: Membrane binding of MreBGs is direct and mediated by the hydrophobic α2-β7 loop protruding from the protein in domain IA.
source: Membrane binding of MreBGs is direct and mediated by the hydrophobic α2-β7 loop protruding from the protein in domain IA
evidence: Inferred from deletion mutant experiments (Figure 4).

claim: MreBGs membrane binding is also mediated by the hydrophobic N-terminus, which together with the spatially closed α2-β7 loop would constitute a membrane anchor.
source: However, we found that MreBGs membrane binding is also mediated by the hydrophobic N-terminus, which together with the spatially closed α2-β7 loop would constitute a membrane anchor
evidence: Inferred from deletion mutant experiments (Figure 4).

claim: MreBGs membrane binding is mediated by electrostatic interactions, possibly through the positively charged residues around the membrane insertion hydrophobic region.
source: as well as by electrostatic interactions, possibly through the positively charged residues around the membrane insertion hydrophobic region.
evidence: Inferred from QCM-D experiments with different lipid compositions and salt concentrations (Figure 3C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).

claim: The absence of an amphipathic helix and the presence instead of a hydrophobic N-terminus in many MreB sequences suggest that most MreB use one or the other amino-terminal structure to bind to membranes.
source: The absence of an amphipathic helix and the presence instead of a hydrophobic N-terminus in many MreB sequences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) suggest that most MreB use one or the other amino-terminal structure to bind to membranes.
evidence: Inferred from sequence analysis across bacterial species (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: In the absence of lipids, MreBs from Gram-negative bacteria have been reported to assemble into sheets and bundles in the presence of either ATP or non-hydrolysable nucleotides.
source: In the absence of lipids, MreBs from Gram-negative bacteria have been reported to assemble into sheets and bundles in the presence of either ATP or non-hydrolysable nucleotides (Barkó et al., 2016; Esue et al., 2005; Esue et al., 2006; Harne et al., 2020; Maeda et al., 2012; Nurse and Marians, 2013; Popp et al., 2010b; Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Barkó et al., 2016; Esue et al., 2005; Esue et al., 2006; Harne et al., 2020; Maeda et al., 2012; Nurse and Marians, 2013; Popp et al., 2010b; Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2001).

claim: Membrane binding and nucleotide hydrolysis are not a prerequisite for polymerization of MreB.
source: as we found here for MreBGs, indicating that membrane binding and nucleotide hydrolysis are not a prerequisite for polymerization.
evidence: Inferred from observation of sheet formation in solution with non-hydrolyzable nucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: ATP binding and hydrolysis promote effective membrane binding and transition to the double-protofilament conformation of MreBGs.
source: However, our data indicate that ATP binding and hydrolysis promote effective membrane binding and transition to the double-protofilament conformation, as recently suggested for Spiroplasma MreB5 (Pande et al., 2022).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations and supported by citation (Pande et al., 2022).

claim: The critical concentration of actin polymerized with ADP is about 18-fold higher than with ATP.
source: The critical concentration of actin polymerized with ADP is about 18-fold higher than with ATP (Fujiwara et al., 2007; Pollard, 1986)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on actin (Fujiwara et al., 2007; Pollard, 1986).

claim: The critical concentration of Thermotoga and Spiroplasma ADP-MreBs was reported to be approximately threefold and twofold higher, respectively, than that of ATP-MreBs.
source: while the critical concentration of Thermotoga and Spiroplasma ADP-MreBs was reported to be approximately threefold and twofold higher, respectively, than that of ATP-MreBs (Bean and Amann, 2008; Takahashi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Bean and Amann, 2008; Takahashi et al., 2022).

claim: The critical concentration of B. subtilis MreB deduced from light scattering experiments was 0.9 µM regardless of the nucleotide species bound, and even in the absence of nucleotide.
source: In contrast, the critical concentration of B. subtilis MreB deduced from light scattering experiments was 0.9 µM regardless of the nucleotide species bound, and even in the absence of nucleotide (Mayer and Amann, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Mayer and Amann, 2009).

claim: Depolymerisation of the membrane-bound double filaments is stimulated by Pi release.
source: This suggests that depolymerisation of the membrane-bound double filaments is stimulated by Pi release, as F-actin depolymerisation.
evidence: Inferred from kinetic experiments and comparison with actin behavior.

claim: Comparison of the crystal structures of apo and ATP-bound MreBGs shows that only minor conformational changes occur upon nucleotide-binding.
source: Comparison of the crystal structures of apo and ATP-bound MreBGs shows that only minor conformational changes occur upon nucleotide-binding, in agreement with what was observed when comparing crystal structures of MreBCc and MreB5Sc in different nucleotide-bound states (Harne et al., 2020; Pande et al., 2022; van den Ent et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from crystal structure comparison and citations to previous studies (Harne et al., 2020; Pande et al., 2022; van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: The invariability of folding regardless of the bound ligands has also been observed in crystal structures of actin and other members of the actin superfamily.
source: This invariability of folding regardless of the bound ligands has also been observed in crystal structures of actin and other members of the actin superfamily (Schüler, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Schüler, 2001).

claim: ATP hydrolysis might promote small but dynamic structural changes in MreB that cannot be observed in crystal structures, which are locked in a conformation imposed by the packing.
source: ATP hydrolysis might promote small but dynamic structural changes that cannot be observed in crystal structures, which are locked in a conformation imposed by the packing.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on limitations of crystallography.

claim: Different modes of membrane binding depending on the nucleotide state have been suggested for MreB based on molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Different modes of membrane binding depending on the nucleotide state have indeed been suggested for MreB based on molecular dynamics simulations (Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Shi et al., 2020).

claim: MreB has limited affinity for lipids, and nucleotide hydrolysis may induce a conformational change that allows or stabilizes its interaction with the membrane.
source: It is tempting to speculate that MreB has limited affinity for lipids, and nucleotide hydrolysis may induce a conformational change that allows or stabilizes its interaction with the membrane.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental observations.

claim: Membrane interaction of MreB could occur by either a monomeric or an oligomeric form of MreB.
source: Membrane interaction could occur by either a monomeric or an oligomeric form of MreB (Figure 6).
evidence: Speculative reasoning presented in the model (Figure 6).

claim: The weak binding energy of individual membrane binding domains could be overcome by multimerization.
source: It was previously speculated that the weak binding energy of individual membrane binding domains could be overcome by multimerization (Salje et al., 2011), which would favor the latter.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous speculation (Salje et al., 2011).

claim: Binding to lipids would induce a second conformational change that triggers polymerization into double protofilaments.
source: Binding to lipids would induce a second conformational change that triggers polymerization into double protofilaments (Figure 6).
evidence: Speculative reasoning presented in the model (Figure 6).

claim: The double filament conformation might in turn favor Pi release, which would ultimately promote filament disassembly.
source: The double filament conformation might in turn favor Pi release, which would ultimately promote filament disassembly.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental observations.

claim: The ADP-Pi-MreB intermediate would be the long-lived intermediate state within MreB filaments.
source: In this scenario, the ADP-Pi-MreB intermediate would be the long-lived intermediate state within MreB filaments.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on comparison with actin.

claim: In the absence of lipids, the decreased Pi release rate observed may reflect either a reduced Pi dissociation from soluble MreB-ADP-Pi or a reduced ATPase activity of the protein.
source: In the absence of lipids, the decreased Pi release rate observed may reflect either a reduced Pi dissociation from soluble MreB-ADP-Pi or a reduced ATPase activity of the protein.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental observations.

claim: MreBGs filaments are straight and rigid at high KCl concentration, strongly deforming and faceting lipid vesicles.
source: Our cryo-EM data show that MreBGs filaments are straight and rigid at high KCl concentration, strongly deforming and faceting lipid vesicles
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cryo-EM observations (Figure 2G).

claim: At lower salt concentration, MreBGs filaments bend the liposomes into negatively curved vesicles.
source: whereas at lower salt concentration, they bend the liposomes into negatively curved vesicles as previously reported for MreBTm and MreBCc (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cryo-EM observations and citations to previous studies (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).

claim: A recent model postulates that MreB polymers are intrinsically curved and have a strong affinity for negatively curved membranes while avoiding to be positively bent.
source: A recent model postulates that MreB polymers are intrinsically curved and have a strong affinity for negatively curved membranes while avoiding to be positively bent (Hussain et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hussain et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2019).

claim: The presence of a high concentration of KCl could stiffen MreB filaments and/or the lipid membrane, leading to a virtual disappearance of curved liposomes in vitro in these conditions.
source: The presence of a high concentration of KCl could stiffen MreB filaments, as shown to occur for actin filaments (Kang et al., 2012), and/or the lipid membrane, leading to a virtual disappearance of curved liposomes in vitro in these conditions.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and citation to previous study on actin (Kang et al., 2012).

claim: In bacterial cells the intracellular KCl concentration varies, ranging from 100 mM to 800 mM in B. subtilis.
source: Because in bacterial cells the intracellular KCl concentration varies, ranging from 100 mM to 800 mM in B. subtilis (Eisenstadt, 1972; Whatmore et al., 1990)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Eisenstadt, 1972; Whatmore et al., 1990).

claim: The identity of the bound nucleotide may regulate the bending properties of MreB filaments, as it has been shown for actin filaments.
source: The identity of the bound nucleotide may also regulate the bending properties of MreB filaments, as it has been shown for actin filaments, with ADP-bound actin filaments being less stiff than ATP-bound filaments (Isambert et al., 1995).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on comparison with actin and citation (Isambert et al., 1995).

claim: Molecular simulations suggest that MreB filaments exhibit nucleotide-dependent intersubunit bending, yet with straight, ADP-bound and curved, ATP-bound filaments.
source: In agreement with this, molecular simulations suggest that MreB filaments exhibit nucleotide-dependent intersubunit bending, yet with straight, ADP-bound and curved, ATP-bound filaments (Colavin et al., 2014), opposite to actin.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Colavin et al., 2014).

claim: MreBGs could be purified in a soluble form that remained functional for polymerization at concentrations below 13.4 µM (0.5 mg/mL).
source: The protein could be purified in a soluble form (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) that remained functional for polymerization at concentrations below 13.4 µM (0.5 mg/mL).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from purification and polymerization assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: When stored frozen at higher concentrations or when conserved overnight at 4 °C, MreBGs rapidly aggregated and could not be recovered in a monomeric state.
source: When stored frozen at higher concentrations or when conserved overnight at 4 °C, MreBGs rapidly aggregated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and could not be recovered in a monomeric state, consistent with the known tendency of MreB proteins to aggregate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from size exclusion chromatography (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
